---
title: "Simulating data"
description: "Choose concentrations, replicates and noise with simulate_data(), and compare simulated data with the true curve."
---

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.2, out.width = "100%")
```

`simulate_data()` makes synthetic data from a model. It chooses the values of the independent variable, computes the model's dependent variable at each, and adds random noise. Simulated data is useful for learning how a model behaves, for testing a fitting approach on data where you know the true answer, and for planning an experiment (see [Designing an experiment](example-experimental-design.html)).

```{r}
library(enzKinet2)
```

## The basics

You give a model code, its parameter values, and the range of the primary independent variable (`A`, the substrate concentration, or `P` for the binding models):

```{r}
set.seed(1)
data <- simulate_data("MM", params = list(Km = 0.8, Vmax = 12), x.min = 0.1, x.max = 6)
nrow(data)
head(data)
```

By default you get 24 evenly spaced concentrations, one replicate each, with noise whose standard deviation is 5% of each rate. The result is a data frame with one column per variable, the same shape as the data `fit_model()` and `make_plot()` take.

The parameter list must include every parameter of the model (`MODEL_PARAMETERS[["MM"]]`), each greater than 0. Other elements are ignored, so you can pass the `fitted.params` from a fit straight in.

## Choosing the concentrations

`n.samples` sets how many distinct concentrations there are, and `space` sets how they're spaced. Here are six concentrations from 0 to 10 with each option, without noise so only the concentrations matter:

```{r}
concentrations <- function(space, ...) {
  simulate_data("MM", list(Km = 1, Vmax = 10), x.min = 0, x.max = 10,
                n.samples = 6, noise.level = 0, space = space, ...)$A
}
concentrations("linear")
concentrations("exponential")
concentrations("inverse.exponential")
```

- `"linear"` (the default) spaces them evenly.
- `"exponential"` puts more of them at low concentrations. Despite its name, the spacing is quadratic: the values are `x.min + (x.max - x.min) * t^2` for `t` evenly spaced from 0 to 1.
- `"inverse.exponential"` puts more of them at high concentrations. The values are `x.min + (x.max - x.min) * (1 - t^3)`, so they also come out in decreasing order.

### Dilution series

`"dilution.series"` mimics a serial dilution. It starts at `x.max` and divides by `dilution.factor` at each step:

```{r}
simulate_data("MM", list(Km = 1, Vmax = 10), x.min = 0.1, x.max = 10, n.samples = 10,
              noise.level = 0, space = "dilution.series", dilution.factor = 2)$A
```

It stops after `n.samples` concentrations, or before going below `x.min`, whichever comes first. Here the next value, 0.078, would be below 0.1, so there are 7 concentrations rather than 10. `dilution.factor` must be greater than 1.

### Your own concentrations

With `space = "custom"`, `x.range` gives the concentrations directly. They must lie between `x.min` and `x.max`, and `n.samples` is ignored:

```{r}
simulate_data("MM", list(Km = 1, Vmax = 10), x.min = 0, x.max = 10,
              noise.level = 0, space = "custom", x.range = c(0.25, 0.5, 1, 2, 4, 8))$A
```

This is the easiest way to simulate the exact design you plan to run in the lab.

## Replicates

`n.replicates` repeats every concentration. The replicates are stacked: all the concentrations of the first replicate, then all of the second, and so on:

```{r}
set.seed(1)
simulate_data("MM", list(Km = 1, Vmax = 10), x.min = 1, x.max = 3, n.samples = 3, n.replicates = 2)
```

Each replicate gets its own noise.

## Models with an extra variable

The inhibition models (`I`), the two-substrate models (`B`) and the quadratic binding model (`R`) have a second independent variable. Its values come from `z.values`, and data is generated for every combination of concentration and z value:

```{r}
set.seed(1)
inhibition <- simulate_data("CI", list(Km = 0.8, Vmax = 12, Ki = 2), x.min = 0.2, x.max = 6,
                            n.samples = 6, z.values = c(0, 2, 5))
head(inhibition)
table(inhibition$I)
make_plot("CI", data.df = inhibition, x.units = "mM", y.units = "µM/min")
```

`z.values` is required for these models, and its values must be 0 or more. For `"QBK"` the `R` values must be greater than 0. For models without an extra variable, `z.values` is ignored.

## Noise

Noise is added to the dependent variable only (`V` or `FB`); the concentrations are exact.

- With `noise.type = "relative"` (the default), the standard deviation is `noise.level` times the true value, so `noise.level = 0.05` means 5%. Larger rates get larger noise, and a rate of 0 stays at 0.
- With `noise.type = "absolute"`, the standard deviation is `noise.level` for every point, in the units of the dependent variable.
- `noise.level = 0` gives noise-free data.

```{r}
set.seed(2)
relative <- simulate_data("MM", list(Km = 1, Vmax = 10), x.min = 0.2, x.max = 10, n.samples = 12,
                          n.replicates = 3, noise.level = 0.1, noise.type = "relative")
make_plot("MM", data.df = relative, title = "Relative noise (10%)")

set.seed(2)
absolute <- simulate_data("MM", list(Km = 1, Vmax = 10), x.min = 0.2, x.max = 10, n.samples = 12,
                          n.replicates = 3, noise.level = 0.5, noise.type = "absolute")
make_plot("MM", data.df = absolute, title = "Absolute noise (SD 0.5)")
```

With relative noise, the replicates spread further apart as the rate rises. With absolute noise, the spread is the same everywhere.

### Clipping and the truncated normal distribution

Noise can push a value outside the range the dependent variable can take: a rate below 0, or a fraction bound above 1. With `distribution = "norm"` (the default), such values are clipped to the edge of the range, and you get a warning. This binding example has absolute noise of 0.1, so values near full binding often go over 1:

```{r}
set.seed(7)
clipped <- simulate_data("BK", list(KD = 1), x.min = 0, x.max = 20, n.samples = 12,
                         n.replicates = 3, noise.level = 0.1, noise.type = "absolute")
sum(clipped$FB == 1)
```

Several points sit at exactly 1, which real measurements rarely would.

`distribution = "truncated.norm"` is an alternative. It draws the noise from a normal distribution truncated to the valid range, so no value needs clipping and the values spread smoothly up to the edge instead:

```{r}
set.seed(7)
truncated <- simulate_data("BK", list(KD = 1), x.min = 0, x.max = 20, n.samples = 12,
                           n.replicates = 3, noise.level = 0.1, noise.type = "absolute",
                           distribution = "truncated.norm")
sum(truncated$FB == 1)
max(truncated$FB)
```

Neither is perfect. Near an edge, both may shift the average of the data a little away from the true curve, so fits to such data might be slightly biased.

## Reproducible data

The noise is random, so each call gives different data. Call `set.seed()` first to get the same data every time, as every example on this site does:

```{r}
set.seed(123); a <- simulate_data("MM", list(Km = 1, Vmax = 10), x.min = 0.5, x.max = 5, n.samples = 4)
set.seed(123); b <- simulate_data("MM", list(Km = 1, Vmax = 10), x.min = 0.5, x.max = 5, n.samples = 4)
identical(a, b)
```

## Curves are dense, noise-free data

`make_curve()` calls `simulate_data()` with no noise and 250 points, so a curve is simply dense, noise-free data. It takes the same model, parameters and spacing arguments:

```{r}
curve <- make_curve("MM", list(Km = 1, Vmax = 10), x.min = 0, x.max = 10)
dim(curve)
```

## Comparing data with the true curve

Because you know the parameters you simulated with, you can draw the true curve alongside a fitted one. `make_plot()` draws `extra.curve` in black on top of everything else:

```{r}
true_params <- list(Km = 1, Vmax = 10)
set.seed(4)
data <- simulate_data("MM", true_params, x.min = 0.2, x.max = 8, n.samples = 6, noise.level = 0.1)
fit <- fit_model("MM", data, start.params = list(Km = 2, Vmax = 8))

make_plot("MM", data.df = data,
          curve.df = make_curve("MM", fit$fitted.params, x.min = 0, x.max = 8),
          extra.curve = make_curve("MM", true_params, x.min = 0, x.max = 8))
```

The coloured line is the fit, and the black line is the truth. The gap between them is the error that this design and this much noise produce. [Designing an experiment](example-experimental-design.html) repeats this many times to compare designs.
